strengths: AudioX offers unusually broad functionality in one model, covering text-, video-, image-, and audio-conditioned sound or music generation, inpainting, and completion.
The evaluation spans multiple public benchmarks, specialized baselines, an out-of-domain AVVP test, zero-shot image-to-audio generation, objective metrics, and a human study.
The system is practically ambitious: it scales a pretrained diffusion transformer to 2.4B parameters and constructs millions of automatically captioned multimodal training examples.
The paper includes useful ablations of masking location, modality-specific masking ratios, unified versus task-specific training, and different conditioning combinations.
Results are competitive across many settings, with particularly strong distributional metrics for text-to-music, VGGSound text-to-audio, and multimodal music generation.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is modest. The architecture largely concatenates features from established frozen encoders and conditions a pretrained latent DiT; input-level masking is simple and its claimed representation-learning advantage is supported by only a small aggregate ablation.

The central state-of-the-art claim is overstated. AudioX loses to baselines on several important metrics: on AudioCaps it trails Tango 2 in KL and alignment and AudioGen in FAD; on AVVP, MMAudio is substantially better in KL, FD, and alignment; and zero-shot image-to-audio alignment is 0.23 versus Im2Wav's 0.41.

Evaluation does not sufficiently test conditional fidelity. Video-to-audio lacks explicit temporal-synchronization metrics, music completion lacks continuity or boundary-quality measures, and averaging Inception Score across heterogeneous tasks in key ablations obscures task-specific effects.

The human study is under-specified and small: only 25 samples per task and 10 raters are used, with no confidence intervals, significance tests, inter-rater agreement, blinding/randomization protocol, or detailed baseline-selection procedure.

Fairness and reproducibility of baseline comparisons are unclear. The paper does not state whether baseline outputs were regenerated with matched duration, sampling, preprocessing, and compute or taken from released results, and it provides no uncertainty over any quantitative result.

Reproducibility is materially limited by 175.2K proprietary text-music examples, absent code and model artifacts at review time, vague scheduler and architecture details, and the very large training requirement. The caption counts are also inconsistent: the abstract reports 190K and 6M, while the dataset section reports roughly 260K and 5.7M.

The automatically generated captions receive no reported quality audit, filtering analysis, or comparison against human annotations. Potential captioning bias and leakage from dataset keywords may inflate text-conditioned results on the same source domains.

The paper does not adequately discuss licensing, copyright, consent, or misuse concerns associated with millions of music/video clips, proprietary music data, generated captions, and release of a general audio-generation model.

The scope implied by “anything-to-audio” exceeds the evidence: only a limited set of modalities and modality combinations is evaluated, image conditioning is handled as padded video without training, and several advertised combinations receive little or no direct comparison.

Some qualitative evidence is difficult to validate from a static paper, and the spectrogram examples cannot establish perceptual quality. Several methodological and presentation details remain imprecise despite the scale of the empirical claims.

strengths: The paper addresses an ambitious and practically relevant goal: one model supports text-, image-, video-, and audio-conditioned sound or music generation, along with inpainting and completion.

The empirical study covers numerous tasks, datasets, specialized baselines, objective metrics, and a small subjective evaluation. Several results, particularly on VGGSound text-to-audio and MusicCaps text-to-music, are competitive.
The proposed caption resources are potentially valuable: the authors report annotations for roughly 260K audio clips and 5.7M music clips and state that these captions will be released.
The paper provides useful high-level implementation information, including model size, pretrained components, masking ratios, inference steps, and approximate training compute.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited. The architecture largely combines frozen standard encoders, feature concatenation, and a pretrained latent Diffusion Transformer. Input masking is well established, and the paper does not offer a sufficiently novel formulation or analysis to elevate it beyond a large-scale engineering integration.

The multimodal evaluation has a serious target-information concern. Text conditions for VGGSound, V2M, and even the AVVP test split are generated by Qwen2-Audio from the corresponding ground-truth target audio or music. Improvements from adding text therefore do not convincingly demonstrate realistic cross-modal integration or out-of-domain generalization; the text can act as an oracle description of the desired output.

Claims of state-of-the-art performance are overstated. AudioX loses to baselines on many important metrics: for example, AudioCaps T2A alignment and KL, VGGSound V2A KL/IS/FD/alignment, AVVP V2A KL/FD/alignment, and image-to-audio alignment. The paper emphasizes favorable metrics without adequately analyzing these substantial tradeoffs.

Comparisons are difficult to interpret because AudioX uses much more training data, including approximately 5.7M V2M clips and 11.7K hours of proprietary text-music data. There is no data-matched baseline, scaling control, or study separating the effects of architecture, masking, pretrained initialization, and training-data scale.

The central masking evidence is weak. The main strategy ablation reports only one unspecified aggregate evaluation without per-task results, uncertainty, or controlled training repetitions. Important details such as masking granularity, sampling, modality/task mixture weights, and how conditioning enters each DiT block are missing, while the proposed information-leakage explanation is asserted rather than demonstrated.

The user study is under-specified and small: only 25 examples per task and 10 raters are used, with no reporting of recruitment criteria, assignment protocol, randomization, blinding, inter-rater agreement, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a 2.4B-parameter system. The manuscript omits essential preprocessing, optimization, diffusion-schedule, architecture, and evaluation details; relies on unavailable proprietary data; and only promises future code/data release.

There is no meaningful discussion of caption quality or validation despite millions of automatically generated labels. Potential hallucination, systematic label bias, train-test contamination, deduplication, licensing, copyright, and broader ethical issues for large-scale audio/music data are not addressed.

Overall, the breadth and some strong numbers are promising, but the limited novelty, oracle-like caption construction, uncontrolled data advantage, incomplete ablations, and insufficient reproducibility prevent the evidence from supporting the paper's central claims at a top-tier conference.

strengths: AudioX offers unusually broad functionality in one model, covering text-, video-, image-, and audio-conditioned generation, both general audio and music, inpainting, and completion.

The empirical study is extensive: it evaluates numerous tasks, datasets, objective metrics, competitive specialized baselines, and a human study. Results are generally strong, with clear gains on several benchmarks such as VGGSound text-to-audio and MusicCaps text-to-music.

The large-scale caption augmentation effort—approximately 260K audio captions and 5.7M music captions—is potentially valuable to the community, particularly if released with adequate documentation and licensing.

The input-masking experiments provide useful evidence that masking raw modality inputs is preferable to feature masking in this setting. Additional comparisons suggest that unified training and combining modalities can improve performance.
The presentation is clear and visually polished, and the main architecture, training setup, datasets, metrics, and computational cost are described at a useful high level.
weaknesses: The architectural novelty is moderate: the method largely combines pretrained modality encoders, concatenated conditioning, a pretrained diffusion transformer, and modality-specific input masking. Its principal contribution is breadth and scale rather than a substantial technical advance.

Several claims are stronger than the tables support. AudioX is competitive overall but is not consistently state of the art; for example, it trails MMAudio on multiple video-conditioned distribution and alignment metrics, and its AudioCaps text-to-audio results are mixed.

Evaluation fairness and possible dataset leakage require stronger analysis. Captions are generated from the ground-truth audio itself, V2M supplies millions of training examples and the corresponding evaluation benchmark, and split deduplication is not documented. Caption accuracy and diversity are also not validated by humans.

Reproducibility is presently limited: code and caption data are only promised for future release; a substantial proprietary music dataset is used; the number of GPUs and precise training mixture are unclear; and important architectural, sampling, modality-dropout, and preprocessing details are missing.

The ablations are relatively shallow for a 2.4B-parameter system. Several results aggregate Inception Score across heterogeneous tasks, with no variance, repeated runs, significance tests, per-task masking analysis, or controls separating the benefits of model scale, pretrained initialization, dataset scale, masking, and unified training.

The user study uses only 25 examples per task and reports means without confidence intervals or statistical tests. Details about evaluator recruitment, randomization, blinding, audio normalization, and inter-rater agreement are absent.

The paper does not adequately discuss licensing, consent, copyright, dataset biases, or misuse considerations, which are particularly important for six million automatically captioned music clips and proprietary music data. The broad “anything-to-audio” terminology also overstates the demonstrated modality coverage.

strengths: Ambitious unified framework supporting text, video, and audio conditioning across sound-effect generation, music generation, inpainting, and completion.
Large-scale data effort: IF-caps contains roughly 7 million clips with structured annotations for categories, counts, timing, ordering, and musical attributes.

Broad empirical evaluation across several datasets, tasks, objective metrics, instruction-following benchmarks, and a small expert study; performance is particularly strong for text-to-audio, text-to-music, and temporal instruction following.
Useful ablations examine caption sources and the main components of the proposed multimodal fusion module.
weaknesses: The architectural novelty is limited. MAF primarily combines standard gating, learned-query cross-attention, self-attention, and concatenation, while key implementation details such as gate equations, query counts, and modality-specific dimensions are missing.

Several central claims are overstated. AudioX is not consistently state of the art: specialist models outperform it on important video-audio alignment and fidelity metrics, and the experiments do not directly test whether conflicting text and video instructions are jointly followed.

T2A-bench has a substantial evaluation-validity concern: Gemini 2.5 Pro generates the benchmark prompts, produces much of the training supervision, and serves as the automated judge. The paper provides no human validation, agreement analysis, or robustness study for this evaluator. Results on the independent AudioTime benchmark help, but do not fully validate T2A-bench.

Data and evaluation separation is insufficiently documented. The caption sources include complete VGGSound and AVVP test data, and AVVP captions are generated from target audio. It is unclear how leakage is prevented and whether audio-derived captions make text-and-video evaluation unrealistically informative.

Comparisons are difficult to interpret because AudioX uses a 2.4B-parameter model and vastly more training data than many baselines. There are no controlled scale/data-matched comparisons, uncertainty estimates, or statistical significance tests. The claimed unified-versus-specialist advantage is reported only through IS with inadequately specified specialist training.

Reproducibility is presently limited by private music data, reliance on proprietary Gemini annotation and judging, missing annotation prompts and detailed architecture specifications, and promises that code and captions will only be released later.

The expert study uses only 25 prompts per task and reports means without confidence intervals, significance testing, inter-rater agreement, or sufficient information about assignment and randomization.

The paper lacks a substantive ethics and data-governance discussion despite curating millions of video/music samples, including private music data. Copyright, licensing, privacy, annotator/model bias, and possible misuse of generated audio are not addressed.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: one model supporting text-, video-, and audio-conditioned sound and music generation.
The experimental scope is broad, covering several generation and editing tasks, multiple established datasets, numerous automatic metrics, and comparisons with strong specialist systems.
AudioX reports particularly strong results for text-to-audio, text-to-music, and temporal instruction following, including corroborating gains on the external AudioTime benchmark.
The data-source and MAF ablations provide some evidence that richer captions and multimodal fusion improve performance.
weaknesses: The main technical novelty is limited. MAF is a conventional combination of gates, learned-query cross-attention, self-attention, and residual updates atop a pretrained diffusion transformer. Its mathematical and architectural specification is too incomplete to reproduce: gate equations, tensor dimensions, query allocation, temporal alignment, missing-modality handling inside MAF, and conditioning interfaces are not adequately defined.

The MAF evidence is not fully convincing. It adds 60M parameters without a parameter-matched control, its gains over partial variants are often small, and the full module is worse than the no-gate variant on ordering error. This does not support claims that every component is essential or that MAF is the principal cause of the reported gains.

The central instruction-following evaluation has substantial circularity: Gemini 2.5 Pro generates training annotations, creates T2A-bench prompts, annotates model outputs, and judges correctness. Training and evaluation are consequently coupled to one proprietary model's language and judgments. No human validation of the benchmark labels or judge accuracy, alternative judge, or robustness analysis is presented.

The dataset construction is insufficiently audited. The paper does not report systematic annotation-quality measurements, filtering criteria, failure rates, duplicate removal, train-test leakage checks, or human verification. It is also unclear how many clips receive Gemini annotation versus Qwen augmentation and how the claimed seven million samples relate to source clips and augmented captions.

Data provenance and ethics are serious omissions. A large private music corpus is central to training, while licensing, copyright, artist consent, demographic or geographic biases, harmful-generation risks, and safeguards are not discussed. Promising to release captions does not make the underlying audio or full training procedure reproducible.

Several comparisons do not justify the broad SOTA language. On video-to-audio and text-video-to-audio tasks, MMAudio is better on multiple fidelity and alignment metrics, while AudioX leads mainly on selected metrics. Baseline generation settings, clip durations, evaluation implementations, and statistical uncertainty are not sufficiently documented to establish fully controlled comparisons.

The human study is weakly reported: only 25 samples per task are used, baseline selection and assignment are unclear, and there are no confidence intervals, significance tests, inter-rater agreement statistics, or detailed recruitment protocol. Spectrogram-only qualitative figures cannot substantiate perceptual-quality claims.

The claimed cross-modal regularization effect is inferred from modest V2A changes under different caption pipelines, without controlling for annotation distribution, training exposure, or other confounders. The evidence supports correlation, not the stronger mechanistic conclusion stated by the paper.

Reproducibility is below the expected standard for a top-tier acceptance. Code, checkpoints, evaluation outputs, prompts, random seeds, complete sampling details, and the benchmark are only promised; key proprietary services and private training data further prevent independent replication.

The title and conclusions overstate generality: the system handles a predefined set of text, video, and audio combinations rather than arbitrary inputs, and its zero-shot image-to-audio alignment is substantially below the strongest specialist baseline. Overall, the work is ambitious and empirically promising, but the novelty, validation independence, reproducibility, and data-governance deficiencies are too substantial for acceptance.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_sample501_han_medium_20260920T175328Z/scratch/4f04b9668094486da1a6c08891a6fd3f/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} tackles an important problem: unifying text-, video-, and audio-conditioned generation across both sound effects and music in one model.
The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering T2A, V2A, TV2A, T2M, V2M, TV2M, inpainting, completion, and zero-shot image-to-audio generation across several established datasets.

AudioX produces strong results, particularly for text-to-audio, text-to-music, and fine-grained instruction following. The improvements on both T2A-bench and the independently proposed AudioTime benchmark are substantial and consistent across multiple control dimensions.

The large IF-caps resource and its structured annotations for categories, counts, temporal relations, timestamps, and musical attributes constitute a potentially valuable contribution beyond the model itself.

The paper includes relevant specialist baselines, objective and subjective evaluations, and ablations of both the captioning pipeline and MAF components. The finding that richer textual supervision can also improve video-conditioned generation is interesting.

The system design is practical: it builds on a strong pretrained diffusion transformer and introduces a relatively lightweight fusion component rather than requiring a completely bespoke generative architecture.
weaknesses: The architectural novelty is moderate. MAF is described mostly at a high level, and the paper does not compare it against sufficiently strong alternative fusion mechanisms, parameter-matched controls, or simple additional-capacity baselines. Moreover, removing the query mechanism actually improves the reported ordering error, so the claim that every MAF component is integral is too strong.

T2A-bench is generated and judged using Gemini 2.5 Pro, while Gemini-generated annotations also supply important training supervision. This creates a risk of shared-model or stylistic bias. The automated evaluator is not validated against human judgments, and no agreement rates, judge-error analysis, repeated evaluations, or alternative evaluator results are reported.

The human study is under-specified. It uses only 25 samples per task and reports averages without confidence intervals or significance tests; details about rater assignment, randomization, repeated ratings, inter-rater agreement, and the number of judgments per system are absent.

Reproducibility is limited by missing implementation details for MAF, modality dropout and task sampling, dataset-mixture weights, augmentation prompts, optimization schedule, and total training steps. Code and datasets are only promised, while a substantial private music corpus is used.

The provenance and separation of IF-caps require greater clarity. Because captions are derived from datasets also used for evaluation, the paper should explicitly document clip-level deduplication and train/test separation. It also provides no direct human audit of synthetic-caption accuracy or hallucination rates.

Claims of uniformly superior multimodal performance should be moderated. On video-conditioned audio tasks, AudioX trails MMAudio on several distributional and alignment metrics, with particularly lower ImageBind alignment; its clearest advantages are fidelity and text-driven generation.

The term “anything-to-audio” overstates the demonstrated scope: the system supports a fixed collection of text, video, and audio combinations, predominantly for short clips, rather than arbitrary modalities or general audio generation settings.

The paper does not adequately discuss licensing, consent, copyright, or release constraints for the millions of music and video-derived training examples, including the private music data. These concerns matter for a large-scale generative-audio dataset.

Several qualitative results are presented only as spectrograms, which cannot substantiate perceptual quality or semantic adherence without accessible audio examples. There are also minor presentation artifacts, including an unresolved footnote/link marker on the first page.
